lesson.title: Bass Filters: Isolating the Low End with a Low-Pass Circuit
lesson.summary: A bass filter is a low-pass filter tuned to the low frequency end of the audio signal, letting bass frequencies through while attenuating the midrange and treble above it.
lesson.body:
A low-pass filter, built from a resistor and capacitor or an inductor and resistor, passes frequencies below its cutoff frequency largely unchanged while progressively attenuating frequencies above that cutoff. A bass filter is simply a low-pass filter applied to an audio signal and tuned so that its cutoff frequency sits inside or near the bass sub band, roughly 20 Hz to 250 Hz, so that everything below the cutoff, the low, bassy content of the signal, is passed through while midrange and treble content above it is rolled off.

For a simple RC low-pass filter, the cutoff frequency is fc = 1 / (2 times pi times R times C). Suppose a designer wants a bass filter with a cutoff near 100 Hz, right in the middle of the bass sub band. Choosing a capacitor of C = 1 microfarad and solving for the resistor gives R = 1 / (2 times pi times fc times C) = 1 / (2 times pi times 100 times 0.000001) = 1,592 ohms, so a standard 1.6 kilohm resistor is a close fit. Checking the result in the forward direction: fc = 1 / (2 times pi times 1,600 times 0.000001) = 1 / 0.01005 = 99.5 Hz, which confirms the component choice lands within about half a percent of the intended 100 Hz cutoff.

In a strict low-pass filter, everything above the cutoff is eventually cut essentially to nothing, which is fine for isolating a subwoofer channel but too aggressive for a tone control knob on a stereo, where you usually want to boost or cut the bass by a controlled amount rather than remove the rest of the audio signal entirely. For that reason, the bass filter inside a tone control circuit is often built as a shelving filter, a variation on the low-pass idea that flattens out at a fixed boost or cut level below the cutoff instead of continuing to roll off forever. That refinement, and how it combines with a treble filter into a complete tone control, is picked up in the audio tone control section later in this chapter.
